div.p: The Flux Tool converts the counts per second (CPS) of each fit peak into the flux of that energy gamma or x-ray, by accounting for the detector response and the geometry. This information can be useful for dose calculations, record keeping, or for export for specialized applications like density determinations.

ul.li: Peak CPS: the peak area divided by the live time of the foreground spectrum as displayed (i.e., of the samples currently shown, not of the whole file).

Intr. Eff. and Geom. Eff.: the detector's intrinsic efficiency (the chance a gamma crossing the crystal face is recorded in the full-energy peak), and the fraction of the solid angle the crystal face takes up; the two multiply to the efficiency used.
Flux on Det. (ɣ/s): gammas per second crossing the face of the detector crystal - a disk of the detector's diameter, at the distance plus the detector setback (see below).
Flux (ɣ/cm²/s): gammas per cm² per second at the detector face - that is, at the distance you entered. This equals ɣ/4π/s divided by 4πd², unless air attenuation is corrected for (see below).
ɣ/4π/s: the number of gammas per second the source gives off in all directions.

div.p: These are the uncollided gammas after any shielding. That is, if the source is shielded, the ɣ/4π/s is what makes it out of the shielding, not what the source itself emits.

In order for the table to have any entries, you must enter a distance and have a detector response function (DRF) selected. The distance can be entered in nearly any reasonable format (ex. "3.2 cm", "4ft 8in", "5m", etc.), and the DRF can be selected by clicking or tapping on the detector widget in the upper right side of the tool to bring up the DRF selection tool. If either the DRF is not selected, or a valid distance is not entered, there will be a prominent message displayed.

The distance is from the center of the source to the face of the detector (the front of the endcap). The detector crystal sits a little behind the face: the DRF's setback, or for a DRF with a geometry-modeled response, the modeled endcap. This is added to the distance when computing the efficiency, and so is included in ɣ/4π/s and in the geometric efficiency and flux on detector. The flux per cm², however, is given at the distance you entered - the front face of the detector - not at the crystal.

When checked (the default), the ɣ/4π/s column is corrected for the gammas absorbed or scattered by the air between the source and the detector face, so that it is what the source (or its shielding) gives off. The correction is about 1% at 1 m and 9% at 10 m for 662 keV gammas, and about 2% at 1 m and 20% at 10 m for 60 keV gammas; it is smaller at higher energies, and larger for low-energy x-rays. The two flux columns are what actually reaches the detector, so are not changed by this option - which means that when it is checked, ɣ/4π/s is larger than the flux per cm² times 4πd².

The air correction assumes the DRF's efficiency does not itself include air attenuation, as is the case for intrinsic efficiencies, and for absolute efficiencies entered with the option to correct them for air attenuation. If your efficiency was measured at some distance without removing the effect of the air in between, leave this option unchecked, or the air will be accounted for twice.

When a background spectrum is displayed, and it has peaks under the foreground peaks, a "Subtract background peaks" option is shown. When checked, the area of any background peak within one sigma of a foreground peak's mean is subtracted from it, the same way the Activity/Shielding Fit tool does it: the background peak areas are first scaled to the foreground, using the background's display scale factor if you have set one, and otherwise the ratio of live times. Only Gaussian background peaks are used. The CPS column then becomes "Net Peak CPS", and a "Bkg. CPS" column gives the background that was subtracted; if the scale factor used is not the ratio of live times, a note below the table says so. If the background's automated peak search found peaks under your foreground peaks that you have not fit in the background, you will be offered to fit and add them when you check the option.

A fixed-geometry DRF already describes the whole source-detector arrangement, so the distance is not used (and can not be edited), there is no air correction, and the flux on detector, flux per cm², and efficiency breakdown columns are not shown. The ɣ/4π/s column becomes the source's gamma emission rate: ɣ/s for a DRF giving total activity, or ɣ/s/cm2, ɣ/s/m2, or ɣ/s/g for DRFs giving activity per unit area or mass. Such an efficiency is usually made for the specific source, including the attenuation within it and any surrounding materials, so this is the emission rate of the source itself, not the "after shielding" number a far-field DRF gives.
div.h3: Peaks outside the DRF's energy range
div.p: If the DRF states the energy range it is valid for, peaks outside of that range have their energy shown in a warning color, and a message below the table lists them; their efficiency is extrapolated (or held at the value at the end of the range), so their numbers are less certain. In the CSV and copied table, a "Notes" column is added saying which rows are affected.
div.h3: Display levels, copying, and CSV export
div.p: The Simple, Standard, and More options choose which columns are shown. Simple shows the energy, nuclide, and ɣ/4π/s, with uncertainties as percentages; Standard shows the energy, CPS, flux per cm², and ɣ/4π/s; and More also adds the nuclide, intrinsic and geometric efficiencies, and flux on detector.

Since the output of this tool is primarily intended for use outside of InterSpec, you can either export the table to a CSV file, or copy it to your clipboard to paste into other applications by clicking the "Copy" link right below the table. Both include the columns of the current display level, with each uncertainty in its own column. Values are given to the same number of significant figures as in the table: between 3 and 9, chosen from the size of the uncertainty (6 when there is no uncertainty) - one more than the uncertainty justifies. Checking "Select rows" adds a checkbox to each row, so you can choose which rows are copied or exported.

Uncertainties given by this tool combine the statistical uncertainty of the peak area (plus that of any background peak area subtracted, added in quadrature) with the efficiency uncertainty the detector response states of its own (plus, for a geometry-modeled detector, the uncertainty its geometry model adds close to the detector). An uncertainty that is only assumed for a detector response stating none (as for the GADRAS detectors) is not included. A line below the table says what was included. The table shows the two combined; hover over a value to see them separately, and the CSV and copied tables give them separately, as in 0.401 (stat) +- 0.112 (syst).
